analysis.one_liner: Sets up a no-fault office to pay Gulf oil spill claims and locks BP's pledge to pay above the legal cap into its federal lease.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, dying when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Deepwater Horizon rig exploded and spilled oil into the Gulf in April 2010, this bill would have created an office inside the Interior Department to pay damage claims from fishermen, coastal businesses, and Gulf governments quickly and without anyone having to prove BP was at fault. It would also have converted a BP letter promising to pay "all legitimate claims" above the $75 million legal liability cap into a binding amendment to BP's federal oil lease, with unpaid legitimate claims bounced back to BP for immediate payment.
analysis.who_benefits: Gulf Coast residents and businesses hurt by the spill — fishing crews, seafood dealers, tourism operators, coastal property owners, and Gulf state and local governments — who would file claims with a new no-fault office and receive payment within about a month of a final decision, without hiring lawyers for a courtroom fight. Lawyers would be capped at 5 percent of any award.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gulf Coast businesses, fishermen, and coastal governments

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Office of Deepwater Horizon Claims Compensation to pay claims on a no-fault, non-adversarial basis, so a claimant only has to show by a preponderance of the evidence that they were damaged by the spill — not that anyone was negligent.
Covered damages include lost property, lost profits and earning capacity, lost subsistence use of natural resources, and the extra public-service costs borne by Gulf state and local governments.

Directs the Interior Secretary to accept BP's May 2010 letter offering to pay "above $75 million" on "all legitimate claims" as an amendment to the oil lease, and to return to BP for immediate payment any legitimate claim BP failed to pay.
Requires claimant assistance centers in areas with large concentrations of potential claimants and expedited handling of claims involving extreme financial hardship.

analysis.who_pays: BP and, through it, the offshore oil industry, which would owe unlimited payment of documented legitimate economic claims. The Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund — financed by per-barrel taxes on oil — would cover the program's administrative costs. Claimants who took the administrative award would give up their right to sue in court over the same damages, including any punitive damages a jury might have awarded.
analysis.who_pays_short: BP, oil-lease taxpayers through the spill fund, and suing claimants

drawbacks.text: The bill stays (freezes) all spill-related damage lawsuits in federal and state court, and claimants have 60 days to elect between the administrative program and the courtroom. A claimant who takes the no-fault award gets no punitive damages, and awards are limited to the economic damage categories the bill lists — less than a jury might have awarded for a spill of this scale.
A five-year deadline applies from when a claimant first could have discovered the damage; claims not filed in time are extinguished entirely.

The liability title does not raise the Oil Pollution Act's $75 million cap for any other company or future spill — it converts one BP letter into a lease amendment, leaving the underlying cap intact and making BP's payment duty depend on the Secretary's finding that claims are "legitimate."

Challenges to the program are funneled to a single court (the D.C. federal courts), with review of awards limited to whether decisions are supported by substantial evidence — a narrower path than ordinary litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Gulf claimants facing years of litigation against a well-funded opponent, fast no-fault payment of documented losses was a real gain, and the bill's fee cap would keep lawyers from taking a large share of awards. The costs are real too: claimants who accepted awards surrendered punitive-damage and full jury-trial rights, the deadline could extinguish late-discovered claims, and the bill's centerpiece liability fix relied on BP's own letter rather than changing the law for anyone else. The bill also inadvertently offered BP something it wanted — a controlled, capped-category payout process instead of open-ended courtroom exposure — which is why a direct statutory liability mandate might have been a stronger design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never taken up — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter of Louisiana introduced the bill on June 7, 2010, six weeks after the Deepwater Horizon explosion, while oil was still flowing.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee; the only other action in the record was an Environment and Public Works Committee hearing on June 9, 2010.
It drew one Republican cosponsor — 1 of 42 Senate Republicans — and no other support in the record.

While the bill sat in committee, BP and the Obama administration negotiated a separate, voluntary $20 billion claims fund administered outside the legislation, which took over the claim-paying role the bill would have formalized.
No further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: BP came out ahead: it ended up paying claims through a voluntary $20 billion fund it negotiated with the administration instead of facing a statute mandating unlimited liability for every legitimate claim, while Gulf claimants were eventually paid through that slower, frequently criticized facility rather than the expedited program this bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: BP, which paid through its own negotiated fund instead

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 7, 2010 to create a no-fault claims office and force acceptance of BP's liability offer.

for.name: 1 of 42 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senator signed on in the record.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 111th Congress by Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-VT)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; it received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after its June 7, 2010 referral.

against.name: BP
against.role: Responsible party for the Deepwater Horizon spill
against.what_they_did: While the bill was pending, agreed with the Obama administration to create a $20 billion escrow claims fund, an alternative that removed the pressure for a legislative claims mechanism.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Pressured BP into the $20 billion claims fund and the claims process that operated in place of spill legislation.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the sponsor was a Louisiana Republican with a single Republican cosponsor, and the record shows no Democratic support or opposition.

industries.industry: BP and offshore oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill would have required BP to pay every documented legitimate economic claim with no liability cap, but it also funneled claims into a no-fault process that excludes punitive damages and jury trials — the litigation shelter the industry values. BP instead negotiated its own $20 billion voluntary fund with the administration while the bill sat in committee.

industries.industry: Gulf fishing, seafood, and tourism businesses
industries.note: These businesses and their workers stood to receive expedited no-fault payment for lost profits, earning capacity, and subsistence use, with claimant assistance centers and fast-track handling for hardship claims.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' attorneys and the tort system
industries.note: The bill caps attorney fees at 5 percent of awards, freezes pending spill lawsuits, and requires claimants to choose between the administrative program and court — pulling business away from litigation over the spill.

industries.industry: Taxpayers through the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund
industries.note: The fund, financed by per-barrel taxes on oil, would cover all administrative costs of the claims office without further appropriation, though damage awards themselves would be paid by the responsible party.
